yarn-troppo.meaning: Every figure and step survives, with litre conversions added: "more than 9,300 gallons (about 35,200 litres)", "a two-hour stretch when nobody's using any water", "replacing at least every five years". Asides react to the text: "Every single day!", "Not bad for an arvo's tinkering.", "which is a bit spooky at two in the morning". No new facts.
yarn-troppo.sense: Terms fit: "down the gurgler" for wasted water, "dunny flappers", "drippy taps", "cistern", "Have a squiz", "a good once-over", "the folding stuff" for money, "easy as".
yarn-troppo.authenticity: Natural, chatty Aussie: "Have a squiz at your water use", "if you haven't chucked it", "get onto an experienced handyperson". "Good news, but:" puts the sentence-final "but" mid-sentence, a slightly forced line.
yarn-troppo.register: Level 4 throughout: a talked-through guide with "No word of a lie", "down the gurgler", "dunny", "squiz", "gotcha". No swearing, within vulgarity 1.
yarn-troppo.tone: Still a helpful how-to, but the extra gags ("gotcha: you've got a leak", "a bit spooky at two in the morning") make it a bit jokier than the original's earnest public-service tone.
yarn-troppo.flow: Reads well aloud, though asides interrupt: "Pipe tape, also called teflon tape, you can get at most hardware shops, it's easy as to put on, and it can help keep leaks in check." is a run-on.
yarn-troppo.variety: Varied: "usual suspects", "sniffing out leaks", "Have a squiz", "once-over", "gizmo", "heaps of tutorials"; "dunny" recurs, but it is the subject.
yarn-troppo.essence: Unmistakably the EPA leak guide, headings and tips intact: "Tip: Don't forget to turn off the water line before you start!"

engine.meaning: Mostly the original verbatim, but two swaps garble it: "wash 60 heaps of dishes" (loads became a vague "heaps") and "Give a stuff about the width of the flapper".
engine.sense: Wrong senses: "Give a stuff about" is the idiom of caring (usually negated), not "pay attention to"; "60 heaps of dishes" replaces a countable "loads"; "colour rocks up in the bowl" strains. "dunny", "taps", "squiz" fit.
engine.authenticity: Swaps bolted onto US prose: "Identify dunny leaks by placing a few drops of food colouring in the cistern" next to "avoid staining the tank"; "the dunny is flushed" in formal passive.
engine.register: Largely untranslated: the whole "Leak Detection and Flow Monitoring Devices" section and the opening paragraph are the original apart from "dunny" and "taps". Far under level 4.
engine.tone: Mostly the original's neutral tone, jolted by "Give a stuff about the width of the flapper".
engine.flow: Reads like the original, with jarring joins where swaps land: "save water and the folding stuff", "60 heaps of dishes".
engine.variety: Leans on "dunny" repeatedly ("Dunny Leaks", "dunny flappers", "your dunny model") with little else.
engine.essence: What it says is the original, so the guide is intact: "Tip: Don't forget to turn off the water line before you start!"

dinkum-3.meaning: Faithful with conversions: "more than 9,300 gallons (around 35,000 litres)", "a two-hour stretch", "at least every five years". Small shifts: "plenty of how-to videos online" narrows "tutorials", and "handyman" for "handyperson".
dinkum-3.sense: Terms fit: "down the gurgler", "usual suspects", "Have a squiz", "once-over", "gizmo", "the folding stuff", "get onto".
dinkum-3.authenticity: Sounds like a local: "Here's a few tips", "down the hardware shop", "Swapping one over is a quick, easy fix". "turn the water off at the line" is slightly odd.
dinkum-3.register: Level 4: conversational throughout with "No word of a lie", "down the gurgler", "dunny", "squiz". Within vulgarity 1. A touch less slang-dense than a full level 4 might be.
dinkum-3.tone: Keeps the helpful how-to tone, friendly without gags: "Make sure you flush straight after, or it'll stain the cistern."
dinkum-3.flow: Smooth and tidy: "You can fix some leaky showerheads by making sure the showerhead's on nice and tight to the pipe stem, with some pipe tape to hold it."
dinkum-3.variety: Varied: "usual suspects", "track down", "pop a few drops", "once-over", "gadgets", "gizmo"; "gadgets" repeats in one section.
dinkum-3.essence: The guide entire, headings and tips: "Tip: While you're at it, it's a good idea to check the washer or \"o\" ring".

yarn-dinkum.meaning: Faithful with accurate conversions: "more than 9,300 gallons (about 35,200 litres)", "50 gallons (about 190 litres)", "500 gallons (about 1,900 litres)". Nothing invented.
yarn-dinkum.sense: Terms fit: "usual culprits", "dead easy", "Have a squiz", "dunny", "the folding stuff", "get onto".
yarn-dinkum.authenticity: Natural: "These sorts of leaks are often dead easy to fix", "the showerhead's on nice and tight"; "Go over the tap gaskets" fine.
yarn-dinkum.register: Lighter end of level 4: "down the drain" rather than a local phrase, and much of the devices section stays formal: "the benefits of installing leak detection and flow monitoring devices". Within vulgarity 1.
yarn-dinkum.tone: Keeps the original's helpful, earnest tone.
yarn-dinkum.flow: Smooth, with one run-on: "Pipe tape, also called teflon tape, you can get at most hardware shops, it's easy to put on, and it can help keep leaks under control."
yarn-dinkum.variety: Modest variety; leans on "get their heads around", "dunny" and "heads-up" but nothing over-used.
yarn-dinkum.essence: Unmistakably the guide, all sections intact.

unharnessed.meaning: All points survive: "more than 9,300 gallons of water a year", "two-hour stretch", "replace it at least every five years", "60 loads through your dishwasher". "forever causing leaks" for "frequently" is a mild overstatement.
unharnessed.sense: Mostly apt: "chew through", "a doddle", "clapped-out toilet flappers", "where the bugger's coming from", "get on the blower", "get stuck in". "a bit of coin" is US-ish for money.
unharnessed.authenticity: Mostly natural, but a few non-Australian picks: "a doddle" is British, "a bit of coin" is American; "strewth!" is bolted on: "enough water for more than 180 showers, strewth!"
unharnessed.register: Level 4 with a dad-level swear used naturally: "track down where the bugger's coming from". Within vulgarity 1.
unharnessed.tone: Friendly how-to tone kept; "strewth!" and "bugger" add a bit of colour without making it flippant.
unharnessed.flow: Smooth: "Most of these are a doddle to fix, needing only a few tools and bits of hardware that'll pay for themselves in water savings."
unharnessed.variety: Well varied: "chew through", "chucking away", "Suss out", "once-over", "clapped-out", "get on the blower", "get stuck in".
unharnessed.essence: The guide entire; fixes the original's garbled list to "home improvement retailer".
